I do not know that 1 have explained with respect to the six months, and perhaps I should do it now. The increased charges in the motive power department for the six months of 1904 from July to December, compared with the corresponding six months of the previous year, and amounting to $261,000, are principally accounted for by the larger amount of traffic handled. This increased traffic is indicated by a much greater locomotive and car mileage, amounting to from 12 to 14 per cent ; a greater amount charged against wages of engine crew, $70,400 during the six months as compared with the like six months of the preceding year. That is due, one-half to the increased engine mileage, and one-half to the higher rates of wages. The heavier traffic involved an increased consumption of fuel to the value of $125,000, and of oil, waste and so forth, to the value of $4,800, thus accounting for the increased expenditure during six months between July 1st *and December 31st last as compared with the like period between July 1st, 1903, to January 1st, 1904. This is partly accounted for by the increased engine mileage, it being 4,690,000 for the six months of 1904 as against 4,050,000 for a like period in 1903. In 1903 the receipts for eleven months were $5,790,876 ; expenses, $5,720,550. This shows a: profit for the eleven months ending May 31, 1903, of $70,317.63, as against a loss during eleven months of 1904 of $585,382.39. It also shows that the receipts for the eleven months ending May 31, 1904, were $5,621 in excess of the same period in the previous year.

Applying the same system of calculation this year the deficit will be in the neighbourhood of $1,500,000. However, the fact remains that for the last four years we have been expending on capital account on the Intercolonial Railway an average of over $3,000,000 a year, and we have a larger deficit besides. Now, when is this going to end? The hon. gentleman says that we cannot help it-that the only prospect in the near future is that when the Intercolonial has the proper equipment there will be an increased revenue. He says that the reason for the deficits is that from Montreal to Halifax the Intercolonial runs along the St. Lawrence river and along the sea coast. The modem idea is that a canal along the line of a railway assists the railway instead of being an injury to it financially. Probably the most prosperous railways we have in Canada run along the St. Lawrence river. Is this thing to go on for ever? Are we always to have a capital expenditure of over $3,000,000 a year and a deficit of over $1,000,000 upon the Intercolonial Railway-a road which was managed by myself with entirely different results. We have also the extraordinary statement of the hon. gentleman that this road could not carry the freight which offered last year for lack of freight cars and locomotives, and that to equip the road fully we require seveuy-five more locomotives. Yet it was only about a year and a half ago that there was such a plethora of locomotives that the Intercolonial Railway was able to lease 36 to the Canadian Pacific Railway. What amount of

increased freight has there been during the last year ? Looking at the figures I find that there has been a very small increase. The hon. gentleman says that the increased expenditure is occasioned partly by the increased cost of mechanical repairs-that he has to pay more for engineers and workmen than formerly. This is a pretty state of affairs.

The hon. gentleman and his predecessor have been furnished to any extent with new locomotives and freight cars, and yet expenses for repairs are greater now than ever they were in the past. He states too that one of the reasons for the large expenditure is that you have to pay the men modern wages. Well, we heard the same thing last year. He then accounted for the deficit by saying he had to pay men up to the standard paid by the Canadian Pacific Railway and other railways. Have we got an increased standard now? Has the standard increased since last year to such an extent that he is enabled to account for the deficit between this year and last by the increased expenditure on this head. But the generosity of the hon. minister is easily accounted for. He says that in December- perhaps it was in November-occurrences happened which caused him to make an arrangement that I think is without precedent in any railway management or corporation in this or any other country-an arrangement under which he only provided for an increase of wages in the future, but for an increase during the six months past. That is a generosity which no doubt should commend itself to the Canadian people ? The particular time in which these occurrences happened is rather significant. True, the hon. minister said it was the beginning of December, but I am strongly inclined to believe that though the Order in Council may have been passed at that particular time, the understanding, from one end of the road to the other, was that the men were to receive six months increase of pay on account of the severity of the fall or the piobable severity of the winter which was to follow.

I tell him that the through freight over the Intercolonial Railway, notwithstanding its extension to Montreal, notwithstanding its right to pass over the bridge into Montreal, is less than it was fifteen or sixteen years' ago. ,Liberal,,Henry Robert Emmerson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae&Language=E&Section=ALL
169955,ca.proc.d.1905-03-01.8.2.40,1905-03-01,0161da2d-c63a-468c-a51e-070c1f9ee40f,ca.m.3700,Mr. HAGGART.,,SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY, ANNUAL STATEMENT.",JL 1 CUIAIUBH.,,"He says there was noloss, but he must take into account the amount of passengers and freight it takes from the other express train on the Intercolonial Railway from Montreal to Halifax. I have heard railway experts say that the loss to the country for the time the hon. gentleman has been running that train, say five months in the year, would be $225,000. It is all very well to give the finest possible accommodation to people travelling on that road, and the people in this section of the country have no objection to anything of the kind, but what we require is that there shall be some economy in management and some reasonable proportion between expenditure and revenue. There can be no justification for saddling this enormous deficit on the surplus earnings of the people of this country ; and no sane man will for a moment entertain the idea that this $4,000,000 of

a deficit could not. be much better expended than losing it in that sink hole, the management of the Intercolonial Railway. The hon. gentleman has made a candid statement. Every year we have had promises from this government of more economical administration and less unsatisfactory results, but, as I shall show at another stage, the expenditure has been increased from year to year. Take for instance the Prince Edward Railway road, on which there has been no increase in the mileage. From 1888 up to 1898 there was an expenditure on capital account of only about $8,300 and since then it has amounted to $17,541 in 1898, $22,000 in 1899, $53,000 in 1900, $280,000 in 1901, $829,000 in 1903 and $098,000 in 1904. I suppose that includes the branches built to that road. In 1S90-91 the working expenses were $257,990 and the gross earnings $174,258. In 1891-92 the working expenses were $289,706 and the gross earnings $157,442. But let us come down to modern years. In 1900-01 the working expenses were $261,766 and the gross earnings $193,833. The following year the working expenses were $270,159 and the revenue $197,999. In 1902-03 the working expenses were $259,637 and the gross revenue $217,714. Last year, 1903-04, the working expenses increased to $335,693, as compared with gross earnings of $234,-3yU, showing a deficit of $100,000 in that one year. This is but a sample of the inmease in the working expenses and in deficits on all the railways under the control of the government. The hon. gentleman says he is going to remedy these things in the future when he has sufficient rolling stock.

He requires at least seventy-five locomotives in order to furnish an efficient service. But he does not think it likely that he will get more than twelve locomotives a year. That is, six or seven years must pass by before he can have the road in what he considers an efficient working condition. Last year the hon. gentleman got twelve locomotives and about $1,000,000 for capital expenditure. The year before he got $3,000,000 or $4,000,000. In order to get the road up to the standard the hon. gentleman contemplates we must expect a large expenditure. But it is noteworthy that both the hon. gentleman and his predecessor have carefully avoided telling the House and the country what these proposed improvements will cost, or when we may hope to have the road upon a paying basis. For my part, 1 protest against all this. I believe that, with proper management, but without increase of the passenger rates or the freight rates, the road could be operated without a single cent of deficit. I know parties who looked into the matter, and they came to the conclusion that, with ordinary good business management, the road ought to yield good returns. And they were willing to take over the road and pay a handsome sum for it, believing that good profits would accrue under efficient management. There is no reason why Mr. HAGGART.

the Intercolonial Railway should be used as a political engine to further the ends of hon. gentlemen opposite. Any advantage from such a course must soon cease. The time will come when the repetition of these things to win political favour will be a weakness rather than a strength. If the hon. gentleman wishes to show successful management, let him run the road as other roads are run. Look at the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Grand Trunk Railway, the Canadian Northern-look at every enterprise in the country that is managed on commercial lines. For the last two or three years the condition with them has been one of plethora. But we find the reverse on the Intercolonial Railway. That road has been going from bad to worse. If the present negligent, loose management continues, instead of a deficit of $4,000,000 a year, we may find the operation of the road to cause even greater loss to the people of Canada.

169994,ca.proc.d.1905-03-01.8.2.79,1905-03-01,dd99b0fc-3398-4c78-a44a-c8ff6a7e9f2e,ca.m.6832,Mr. KEMP.,,SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY, ANNUAL STATEMENT.",JL 1 CUIAIUBH.,,"I see that in the months of November and December, 1903, and January and February, 1904, there was a considerable amount of grain carried from Parry Sound to Halifax for export, wheat and corn The arrangements which were made with the Intercolonial required the rate of freight to be divided between the three roads over which this grain *went, the Canada Alantic Railway, the Grand Trunk Rail wav and the Intercolonial. One rate was 515, another 4'90, and in one case, 4'94. I see 31,836 bushels were carried from Parry Sound to Halifax, at 4 90 per bushel. Now the mileage was 346 miles for the Canada Atlantic Railway, 34 for the Grand Trunk, and 828 for the Intercolonial. The rate was divided in this way : The Canada Atlantic Railway received their share 2:15 cents, the Grand Trunk. Railway -60 aud the Intercolonial Railway 215, exactly the same as the Canada Atlantic Railway while the Canada Atlantic Railway mileage was 346 miles and the Intercolonial Railway mileage was 828 miles. Is that a proper way in which to conduct this kind of business ? Can the Intercolonial Railway enter into a bargain of that kind and consider that it is profitable ? I would like to have an explanation from the hon. minister.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Albert Edward Kemp,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=dd99b0fc-3398-4c78-a44a-c8ff6a7e9f2e&Language=E&Section=ALL
169995,ca.proc.d.1905-03-01.8.2.80,1905-03-01,05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae,ca.m.1687,Mr. BMMERSON.,Minister of Railways and Canals,SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY, ANNUAL STATEMENT.",JL 1 CUIAIUBH.,,"I can easily give the explanation that has already been given to this House. That was a transaction iu connection with the carrying of certain traffic to Halifax and at the same time the bringing back of certain imports brought in by steamer to Halifax, and the two together-this traffic going down in the cars and the other traffic coming up in the return cars-made a profitable transaction for the Canadian Pacific Railway. That transaction was deemed to be, from the financial standpoint, in the interests of the Canadian Pacific Railway, taking into consideration the traffic that came in by the steamers at Halifax and was transported to Montreal and other ports.

,Liberal,,Henry Robert Emmerson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae&Language=E&Section=ALL
169996,ca.proc.d.1905-03-01.8.2.81,1905-03-01,dd99b0fc-3398-4c78-a44a-c8ff6a7e9f2e,ca.m.6832,Mr. KEMP.,,SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY, ANNUAL STATEMENT.",JL 1 CUIAIUBH.,,"I may say that I do not take any stock in the explanation which has been furnished the hon. minister in respect to this transaction. This is one instance, and an instance of a similar character occurred a few years ago. The fact of the matter is that the Canada Atlantic Railway did not make very much money on the carrying of that grain 346 miles for 2:15 cents and if that is the case with the Canada Atlantic Railway, what a loss must the Intercolonial Railway have stiffer-Mr. EMMERSON.

ed in carrying it at the same price 828 miles? it stands to reason to my mind that this Is a transaction that will not stand argument on its merits. I say it is a political transaction rather than a business one.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Albert Edward Kemp,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=dd99b0fc-3398-4c78-a44a-c8ff6a7e9f2e&Language=E&Section=ALL
169999,ca.proc.d.1905-03-01.8.2.84,1905-03-01,05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae,ca.m.1687,Mr. EMMERSON.,Minister of Railways and Canals,SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY, ANNUAL STATEMENT.",JL 1 CUIAIUBH.,,"Nobody thought that but somebody who wanted to figure and speculate on elections. But, it does not do away with the statement which I have made on the authority of the traffic manager that the two transactions, the carrying of the traffic down to Halifax and the entering into a contract to bring a certain quantity of imports up to Montreal made it, certainly, if not a very profitable transaction, at least one that was in the interests of the Intercolonial Railway. We had the cars and we had the men, we wanted to give them employment, we wanted the traffic, and if that traffic can be secured and that employment given without serious loss it is to the advantage of the Intercolonial Railway.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Albert Edward Kemp,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=dd99b0fc-3398-4c78-a44a-c8ff6a7e9f2e&Language=E&Section=ALL
170001,ca.proc.d.1905-03-01.8.2.86,1905-03-01,05ffcd85-4168-4656-82c4-05a0c40faaae,ca.m.1687,Mr. EMMERSON.,Minister of Railways and Canals,SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY, ANNUAL STATEMENT.",JL 1 CUIAIUBH.,,"For the reason that all traffic arrangements in connection with the Intercolonial Railway aud all passenger arrangements have to be calculated on the basis of the least mileage ; that is to say that a passenger ticket from Montreal to St. John on the Intercolonial is sold at the same price as a ticket over the Canadian Pacific Railway to St. John, although the route over the Canadian Pacific Railway is much shorter. age and of course it places the Intercolonial Railway at a disadvantage. Mi-. KEMP. The St. John mileage is 346 miles. It is the same mileage as that of the Canada Atlantic Railway, yet the Intercolonial and the Canada Atlantic Railway had exactly the same earnings.

McLEAN.,,SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY, ANNUAL STATEMENT.",JL 1 CUIAIUBH.,,"I would like to make a few remarks on this item with regard to the carrying of grain to Halifax. In the last campaign one of the great arguments used by government candidates was that by the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific to Moncton that road would be in a position to carry freight from the west to Moncton, and that it could be taken from there to the ports of Halifax and St. John by the Intercolonial Railway. If the Intercolonial Railway to-day is not in a position to carry grain, then I think the hon. minister should show to this House to-night when it will he in a position to do so, and what the cost will be in order to make that railway callable of carrying grain. There is no doubt, Mr. Chairman, that this is a great industry, and that the road to-day should be in a position to carry all the grain that can be taken to St. John and Halifax. We have been told for many years in parliament that these two ports were to be the great winter ports of this country, and that Portland, which is now used by the Grand Trunk Railway will not be the port which will be used by the Grand Trunk Pacific but that they

will use St. John and Halifax. I also understood from remarks of the minister and of the hon. gentleman from Lanark (Mr. Haggart) who replied to him that a large amount of money is now required in order to properly equip the line. We also had a statement in the House to-night that we have been spending on capital account during the last seven or eight years, millions of money yearly, not only to keep it up to an efficient condition, but to place it in a more efficient condition than it was before. In 1903, in the matter of passenger cars, which we need not deal with at present, and in the matter of engines and freight cars, the Intercolonial was represented to be one of the best lines in Canada. In that year the Grand Trunk Railway had for every 100 miles of its

railway 775 freight ears, and the Intercolonial 774, a difference of one; and for every 100 miles the Grand Trunk had 22 locomotives and the Intercolonial 21. So that practically these two lines were upon the same basis as regards equipment for carrying freight. Since 1903, the Intercolonial has not been going back, but going forward, by leaps and bounds, in the matter of expenditure on capital account for equipment. Therefore it seems extraordinary that the minister should be in the humiliating jiosition to-night of having to admit that the Intercolonial is practically unable to compete for the carrying trade of the country by reason of not having the necessary means of transportation either in en gines or cars. or anything of that kind, yet its accounts are kept separate, and this does not necessitate any extra officials in any shape or form. There was no distinctive line drawn between that portion of the road and any other. When Sir Charles Tupper, in 1879, bought, as Minister of Railways, the River du Loup branch, there was no distihction made between that branch and the main line. The same course was followed when the St. Charles branch was built. 170073,ca.proc.d.1905-03-01.8.2.158,1905-03-01,7b93f979-f291-49f1-9a5c-54d08800f177,ca.m.2348,Mr. SPROULE.,,SUPPLY-INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY, ANNUAL STATEMENT.",JL 1 CUIAIUBH.,,"But the argument that was put forward when we where asked to vote money for the extension of it is what I have stated. When the Drummond County Railway was purchased, we were told that it was to bring the Intercolonial Railway up to the grea t metropolis of Montreal where it would gather freight to make it a paying road. And we were told that when the accounts were analysed it would be found a paying part of the road and would help to put the Intercolonial on a paying basis. And, last year, when the Canada Eastern was purchased, we were told that it would help to make the Intercolonial pay. But when the government went to the country in the general election, one of the arguments advanced from that side was that the Intercolonial never had and never would pay, and so the government would not be justified in undertaking to build and operate a transcontinental line as proposed by the leader of the opposition. It was said that the more branches we purchased for the Intercolonial the worse it would be. I made up my mind either that the arguments presented in support of purchasing the Canada Eastern were misleading and improper, or those who used them were dishonest in that use, or else that they were wholly ignorant of what would take place. We have not the advantage of time to prove the correctness of our policy, but we can only reach the conclusion that the government were very unwise in buying the Drummond County road if the Intercolonial was running farther aud farther behind. And the same was true of the Canada Eastern.

Every one knows that the Intercolonial Railway has not been doing a very paying business for the last few years, or'in fact, since its inception, but on the other hand, not many people know that in Montreal the fish dealers are paying a large amount per week to the Grand Trunk Railway Company for the transportation of fresh fish from Boston, or Portland to Montreal.
